title: 8 Costly Vacation Rental Expense Management Mistakes to Avoid in 2026
summary: Don't let cost creep or manual tracking ruin your margins. Learn the 8 critical expense management mistakes STR managers make and how to automate for profitability in 2026.
body_text: Introduction: Why Expense Management Will Define STR Profitability in 2026 Talk to any vacation rental operator today and you’ll hear the same story: reconciliation is messy, expense tracking is inconsistent, and financial workflows have quietly become one of the biggest bottlenecks in STR operations. And the pain is real. It's January 3rd, and your phone is lighting up. Three owners are questioning charges on their December statements. Your bookkeeper is chasing down receipts from November. And you still can't explain why one property shows a $4,200 maintenance bill when similar units averaged $1,800. This is the reality for thousands of operators heading into 2026. Margins are tightening as insurance costs continue to climb, labor becomes more expensive, booking pace stabilizes after post-pandemic spikes, and competition rises in nearly every major market. Meanwhile, owner expectations have evolved. They don't just want payouts—they want transparency, timely reporting, and documentation they can trust. In short: financial discipline is no longer "back-office work." It's a strategic differentiator that determines owner trust, portfolio profitability, and your ability to scale. This post breaks down the 8 most common—and costly—expense management mistakes property managers make, and how to fix them before they impact profitability, compliance, or growth. Mistake #1: Disorganized, Manual Expense Tracking Why is manual expense tracking the biggest bottleneck for STR growth in 2026? Many property managers still rely on scattered, manual processes to track expenses—and it catches up fast. Receipts live across text threads from cleaners, emails from vendors, paper slips handed off in the field, photos buried in camera rolls, and scribbled notes that never make it into the system. You probably recognize these scenarios: a cleaner hands you a receipt that disappears before you're back in the office, a maintenance tech buys supplies with a personal card and forgets to submit the documentation, or peak season creates dozens of undocumented purchases per week that get logged days or weeks after they occur—if they get logged at all. This creates two hidden issues operators rarely catch early. First, there's no real-time visibility—you don't know how much you actually spent this week until month-end closes, which means overspending isn't caught until it's too late. Second, expenses aren't tied to work orders, so a $240 "hardware store" expense shows up with no job reference, making owners question charges and forcing staff to scramble to justify them weeks after the fact. The downstream effects are worse: missed reimbursements that hurt team morale, duplicate charges to owners, month-end delays while chasing missing documentation, inaccurate owner statements, and frustrated bookkeepers who become human detectives instead of strategic finance partners. Owners lose confidence when they can't see receipts attached to every charge. And in 2026, with portfolios growing and teams stretched thin, these manual gaps become exponential problems. How to Fix It Centralize receipt documentation from day one (one system, not seven). Use mobile receipt capture tools or corporate card systems with auto-categorization. Tie every expense to a work order or job ID to eliminate disputes. Train field teams: "No receipt = no reimbursement". Standardize naming conventions for receipts, vendors, and notes. Review receipts weekly, not monthly, to catch gaps early. Getting Team Buy-In Your field teams won't adopt new processes just because you announce them. Here's how to get buy-in: For cleaners and maintenance staff: Frame it as protecting them, not punishing them. "We're implementing this so you never miss a reimbursement again. No more chasing down payments or questioning what you're owed." Make the new process easier than the old one—a mobile app that takes 30 seconds beats texting photos that disappear into message threads. For vendors: Set clear expectations upfront. "Starting next month, all invoices need itemized receipts and work order numbers. Without these, payment will be delayed. This protects both of us and ensures you get paid faster once we receive complete documentation." Build it into your vendor agreements from day one. For internal staff: Show them the time they'll save. "We spent 12 hours last month hunting down receipts and reconciling unclear charges. This new system eliminates that entirely and lets you focus on higher-value work." Celebrate early adopters publicly—recognition drives long-term compliance. The tax compliance advantage: Digital expense tracking also protects your 1099 contractors during tax season. With IRS 1099-K thresholds now at $600, contractors without organized documentation face reconciliation nightmares come April. Real-time digital tracking gives your field staff audit-ready records for their Schedule C deductions—turning shoeboxes of receipts into automatic tax preparation. Position your system as their personal tax assistant, not just your accounting tool. The Real Cost of Disorganization The financial impact of manual tracking compounds faster than most operators realize. A 50-unit portfolio losing just $50 per property per month to expense leakage, duplicate charges, and missed reconciliations equals $30,000 annually. For a 150-unit operation, that number jumps to $90,000—enough to hire another full-time employee or fund a complete tech stack upgrade. Time costs matter just as much. Operators report spending 10-15 hours per month chasing missing receipts and correcting errors. At a conservative $50/hour labor cost, that's $6,000-$9,000 in wasted time annually for a mid-sized operation. That's time your team could spend on revenue-generating activities like owner acquisition or operational improvements. Mistake #2: PMS, Bank, and Accounting Systems Aren't Properly Reconciled How do you fix the "Three-Way Reconciliation" nightmare between PMS, Bank, and Accounting? Vacation rental operators rely on three separate systems to manage expenses: your PMS (Guesty, Hostaway, Streamline, OwnerRez, Track, etc.), bank accounts, and accounting software (QuickBooks, Xero). When these systems don't sync correctly—or at all—financial chaos follows. The failure points are predictable but painful. Manual data entry causes discrepancies. Timing differences emerge between PMS posting and bank clearing. Chart-of-accounts mismatches create confusion when "Cleaning" in one system becomes "Housekeeping" in another. PMS pass-through expenses don't sync into accounting at all. Multi-line invoices sync as a single lump sum instead of per-property splits. Sync errors go unnoticed until month-end. Bank rules or feed issues change without warning. The result is hours of manual reconciliation every month, balance sheet inaccuracies that compound over time, incorrect trust balances, difficulty identifying overspending or cash flow gaps, year-end tax pressure due to mismatches, unreliable owner statements, and audit risk if trust and operating accounts aren't aligned. How to Fix It Establish a weekly reconciliation cadence (not monthly). Audit PMS → accounting mappings quarterly. Review multi-property vendor invoices for proper splits. Double-check that pass-through expenses sync correctly. Document your reconciliation workflow so it isn't dependent on one person. Pro Tip: Set a recurring reminder for Friday at 2 PM to spot-check PMS, bank, and accounting alignment. Catching errors within 7 days is dramatically easier than cleaning up a month's worth of mismatched data. The Real Cost of Poor Reconciliation Operators who reconcile monthly instead of weekly report spending 2-3x more time fixing errors. A weekly 30-minute reconciliation check (26 hours annually) prevents the 40-60 hour year-end cleanup that monthly reconcilers face. That's 14-34 hours saved annually, plus the avoided cost of tax amendments, owner statement corrections, and the reputational damage from inaccurate reporting. For portfolios over 100 units, failed reconciliation can create trust account discrepancies of $10,000-$50,000 that take months to unravel. Mistake #3: Incorrect Allocation of Owner Expenses Why do incorrect owner expense allocations lead to high churn rates? Incorrectly charging expenses to the wrong unit or owner is one of the fastest ways to lose trust, and one of the hardest mistakes to recover from in STR management. This often happens because of similar or confusing addresses (Main St. vs. Main Ave.), multi-property work orders where costs aren't properly split, rush jobs that get logged without verification, vendors using vague or generic invoice descriptions, expenses logged without a work order or job reference, and warranty-covered or owner-provided items mistakenly charged. The fallout is costly and extends far beyond the immediate error. You face immediate owner disputes, time-consuming statement corrections, hours of staff time wasted tracking down what happened, incorrect property profitability reporting, and long-term erosion of trust. Potential churn follows, especially among luxury, institutional, or multi-home owners who expect precision. Consider this example: A 150-unit manager discovered lawn care for Property A was billed to Property B for six consecutive months, requiring 14 hours of corrections and straining a previously strong owner relationship. How to Fix It Require property ID + owner name + work order ID before finalizing any expense. Use templates for recurring expenses (lawn care, cleaning, HVAC service plans). Implement a peer review for high-dollar items. Create a standardized naming convention across PMS + accounting. Flag and review any vendor invoice that includes multiple properties or unclear descriptions. How to Communicate Corrections to Owners When you discover a misallocated expense, own it immediately and make the correction transparent: Sample message: "Hi [Owner Name], we discovered an accounting error where a $180 lawn care charge for 123 Main St was incorrectly posted to your property at 456 Oak Ave. We've corrected this on your January statement, and you'll see a $180 credit. We've also implemented a new verification step in our expense approval process to prevent this going forward. Please let me know if you have any questions." Key elements: acknowledge the error clearly, explain what happened without making excuses, show exactly what you've fixed, and demonstrate you've improved the process to prevent recurrence. Never blame your team publicly, own it as a company-level issue. Mistake #4: Commingling Trust Funds With Operating Accounts Why is Commingling Trust and Operating accounts a risk in 2026?" Many property managers still mix owner funds (trust accounts) with business operating funds. This is one of the biggest compliance and financial risks in the vacation rental industry, yet it often goes unnoticed until an audit, owner dispute, or regulatory issue forces the problem into the open. Commingling creates a cascade of problems that compound over time. It can lead to legal violations in states with strict trust requirements, failed audits or regulatory issues, owner disputes over incorrect payouts, chargebacks pulling from the wrong account, refunds being paid using owner money, inaccurate cash flow reporting, negative trust balances during high-refund periods, and difficulty answering the fundamental question: "How much belongs to owners vs. the company?" The operational confusion deepens when security deposits and damage waivers get misclassified and spent early, PMS payout adjustments don't align with bank deposits, and owner distributions are incorrect because liabilities are unclear. Red Flags You're Commingling Watch for these warning signs: Paying payroll, rent, software, or marketing from owner funds. Depositing guest payments and company revenue into the same account. Using operating funds for refunds or chargebacks. Failing to track security deposits separately. Struggling to identify accurate trust balances. How to Fix It Open separate accounts: one for operating, one (or more) for trust funds. Understand your state's trust accounting rules (some require separate accounts per owner). Use your PMS or accounting software to track trust liabilities per property. Train your team on which transactions belong to which account. Reconcile trust accounts weekly to ensure accuracy. Trust Accounting 101 ‍ Trust funds equal money held on behalf of owners (rent, security deposits, damage waivers, owner reimbursements). Operating funds equal money belonging to your management company (management fees, commission revenue, your business income). These must never mix, not even temporarily. Pro Tip: Security deposits and damage waivers are not the same, and treating them as identical can create trust accounting violations. Security deposits are liabilities and must remain in the trust account until released or applied. Damage waivers are typically non-refundable fees and often belong to the company, meaning they should flow to your operating account, not trust. Clear separation prevents misallocations, failed audits, and owner disputes at year-end. Mistake #5: Inconsistent Vendor Cost Control How does "vendor cost creep" quietly erode property management margins? Vendor cost creep is one of the most expensive, and least-tracked, risks in STR operations. Common situations play out across portfolios every day: a cleaner charges $150 in one month, then $180 the next with no explanation or advance notice. Maintenance vendors submit invoices weeks late, making it impossible to budget accurately. Landscaping costs vary wildly by property or season with no documentation of why. Vendor descriptions are vague ("maintenance" or "supplies"), making audits impossible. There's no standardized scope of work, so vendors charge inconsistently for the same service at different properties. Seasonal surcharges appear without warning. High-dollar repairs happen without prior approval from you or the owner. The financial impact compounds year over year—typically 10–20% annual cost creep that erodes margins without anyone noticing until it's too late. You lose the ability to negotiate confidently because you don't have baseline data. Property-level profitability becomes unreliable. Owners question rising costs without clear justification. Trust erodes when vendors appear out of control. One 150-unit manager we spoke to discovered their cost-per-clean increased from $110 to $142 over 18 months—a $38,000 annual impact—simply because no one tracked it. How to Fix It Create vendor rate cards for every service category. Document a standardized scope of work (SOW) for cleaners, maintenance, landscaping, and pool vendors. Track cost-per-clean, cost-per-booking, and maintenance cost trends. Flag invoices that exceed baselines by 20%+. Conduct quarterly vendor performance reviews using actual data—not gut feel. Implement a pre-approval limit (e.g., any work over $250 requires PM approval or owner consent). Track seasonal pricing to identify and negotiate peak-season increases. Getting Vendor Buy-In on Documentation Standards Vendors will resist new requirements if you spring them without context. Here's how to introduce changes: Initial conversation: "We're improving our expense tracking system to ensure faster payment and fewer disputes. Starting next month, we'll need itemized invoices with work order numbers for all services. This protects both of us—you'll get paid faster with clear documentation, and we can justify charges to owners without back-and-forth confusion." For pushback: "I understand this adds a step to your process, but it actually eliminates the 3-5 day payment delays we've had when invoices are unclear or incomplete. Would you prefer we provide a template you can use, or do you have your own invoicing system that can include these details?" Enforcement: After the transition period, delay payment on non-compliant invoices with a brief note: "Invoice received, but we need the work order number and itemized breakdown to process payment per our agreement. Can you resubmit by Friday?" Most vendors comply immediately after one delayed payment—they want to get paid on time just as much as you want clear documentation. The Hidden Cost of Vendor Creep That $38,000 annual impact from untracked cost-per-clean increases is just one example. Across a 100-unit portfolio, uncontrolled vendor costs typically create 10-20% annual expense creep. On $2M in vendor spend, that's $200,000-$400,000 over five years—money that quietly erodes profitability without anyone noticing until owner margins become unsustainable and renewals start declining. Operators who implement quarterly vendor reviews report identifying $15,000-$50,000 in annual savings within the first year, simply by having data-driven conversations with vendors about pricing, scope, and performance. Mistake #6: Missing Documentation or Weak Audit Trails Why are weak audit trails and missing receipts a red flag for modern STR owners? Your accounting system is only as good as the documentation behind it. Yet many expenses are logged with vague, meaningless descriptions like "Supplies," "Hardware store," "Misc.," or simply "Maintenance." Worse, many entries have no receipt attached, no work-order link, and no detail whatsoever about what was purchased or why. This creates major issues that ripple through your entire operation. You might face IRS audit risk. Owners dispute unclear or unsupported charges. You can't validate expenses during monthly or annual reviews. Staff transitions or turnover create confusion because no one knows what past expenses were for. Incorrect categorization affects tax reporting. Repairs get billed without proof of owner authorization. There's no visibility into what was purchased or why. This matters now more than ever because owners expect full transparency. If you can't attach receipts, photos, or the specific work order, they'll lose trust. Internally, missing documentation slows down month-end close and creates massive cleanup work later. How to Fix It Require vendor name, property address, detailed item description, and work-order ID for every expense. Tie every maintenance or cleaning expense to a work order or job ticket. Enforce receipt uploads within 30 days. Capture photos for anything involving materials, repairs, or replacements. Use corporate cards with auto-categorization and forced receipt upload. Create a "No PO, No Pay" policy for vendors who don't follow documentation requirements. Build documentation standards into your staff onboarding and workflow. Getting Team Buy-In on Documentation Your team will see new documentation requirements as "more work" unless you show them what's in it for them: For bookkeepers and finance staff: "This eliminates 80% of the follow-up emails and detective work you currently do each month. Instead of chasing people down for missing information, you'll have everything you need automatically linked when you need it." For property managers and coordinators: "When an owner questions a charge, you'll have the receipt, photos, and work order linked instantly in one place. No more scrambling through emails, text threads, or paper files trying to piece together what happened." For field teams: "This protects you from disputes and confusion. Every expense you submit is documented and approved with a clear trail, so there's never confusion about what was authorized, what was purchased, or what you're owed for reimbursement." Make compliance easy by providing templates, checklists, and mobile-friendly tools. Celebrate teams that consistently submit complete documentation—public recognition drives behavior change. After 30 days, most teams realize the new process is actually faster and less stressful than the old chaos of missing receipts and unclear expectations. Audit Trail Checklist Every expense should include these elements: ‍ Vendor Information: Vendor name, vendor type (cleaning, maintenance, supplies, etc.), and contact information. ‍ Detailed Description: What was purchased or serviced, with line-item detail including materials, labor, quantities, unit cost, and total cost. ‍ Property Details: Property address and property ID (matching PMS and accounting). ‍ Dates: Date of purchase/service and date expense was entered into the system. Expense Category: Why the expense occurred (cleaning, repair, materials, CapEx, PM cost, etc.), and whether it's a repair, replacement, or improvement. ‍ Work Order/Task Link: Work Order ID or task number, linked maintenance or cleaning ticket from PMS, and photos (before/after if applicable). ‍ Receipt/Invoice: Photo or PDF of the receipt that includes vendor name, date, line items, and amount. ‍ Authorization: Owner approval for high-dollar or non-emergency items, timestamp of approval, and name of the approver (owner or PM). ‍ Allocation: Correct owner, correct property, and proper split if multiple properties appear on one invoice. ‍ Accounting Mapping: COA category, sub-account if applicable, and confirmed PMS to Accounting sync or manual entry. Mistake #7: Delayed Expense Recording & Month-End Close How does a slow month-end close cycle damage your reputation with owners? Many teams still batch expenses at month-end. It feels efficient in the moment, but it actually creates massive bottlenecks that slow down the entire financial cycle and create downstream chaos. The root causes are familiar: field teams wait until they're forced to submit expenses rather than doing it in real-time, there's no accountability or consequences for missing deadlines, receipts are missing or incomplete when they finally arrive, approvals pile up in the last 48 hours of the month creating a crushing workload, and expenses get backdated, causing PMS to accounting sync issues that require manual fixes. When expenses come in late, everything downstream slows down. Month-end close stretches to 5–15 days. Owner statements go out late. Cash flow forecasting becomes inaccurate. Property-level profitability reporting is wrong. Trust account balances become unreliable. Owners lose confidence and question your internal controls. Perhaps the biggest owner frustration is the delayed charge problem: "Why am I being billed now for something that happened last month?" Late expenses create "owner gotcha" charges that erode trust, even when the charge is legitimate. How to Fix It Switch to weekly expense reviews (no more month-end pileups). Require expenses to be logged within 5 business days. For field teams: same-day expense entry whenever possible. Use dashboards or alerts to monitor submission timeliness. Implement a "daily micro-close" mindset—light reconciliation throughout the month. Celebrate teams or individuals who consistently hit submission deadlines. Block owners from receiving statements unless all expenses are submitted (forces discipline). Communicating Process Changes to Owners When you tighten expense recording timelines, statements might be delayed by a few days in the first month as your team adjusts to new workflows. Get ahead of owner concerns with proactive communication: Sample announcement: "We're implementing a new financial process that will significantly improve accuracy and speed up our monthly close. You may notice your February statement arrives 2-3 days later than usual as we transition to the new system, but starting in March, you'll receive statements consistently by the 5th of each month instead of the 10th-15th range. This also means fewer corrections, better expense documentation, and more accurate reporting throughout the year." Frame temporary delays as investments in long-term accuracy and consistency, not failures in execution. Most owners appreciate transparency and will support short-term adjustments that lead to better service. The Real Cost of Delayed Expense Recording Late expense recording creates a ripple effect that costs far more than the hours spent fixing it. Operators who batch expenses at month-end report: 5-15 day close cycles vs. 3-5 days for operators with daily/weekly processes 2-3 statement corrections per month vs. less than 1 for proactive teams 15-25 hours of staff time monthly spent chasing receipts and resolving discrepancies For a 75-unit portfolio, switching from monthly batching to weekly reviews saves approximately 120-180 hours annually—equivalent to $6,000-$9,000 in labor costs at standard rates. More importantly, it eliminates the owner frustration that drives churn and negative referrals. Owners consistently rank "timely, accurate statements" as a top-3 decision factor when renewing management contracts. Late statements signal operational weakness and lack of financial control, even when the underlying property management and guest services are strong. Fix your close process, and you'll see retention improve. Example Process Flow ‍ Days 1–5 (Continuous Throughout Month): Expenses occur and are documented in real time. Receipts and work orders are submitted same day or within 5 business days. Corporate card transactions auto-categorize. Field teams complete documentation requirements. ‍ Day 7–9 (Weekly Expense Review): Approve previous week's expenses, correct any missing documentation, match expenses to work orders, and flag outliers for vendor review. ‍ Day 12–15 (Mid-Month Cleanup): Resolve orphaned transactions, follow up on missing receipts, clear outstanding vendor invoices, and ensure PMS to accounting sync is clean. ‍ Last 2 Business Days of the Month: Ensure all expected expenses for the month are submitted and lock internal deadline for field and vendor submissions. ‍ Days 1–2 of the New Month (Month-End Close): Enter final vendor invoices, verify all PMS pass-through expenses, complete bank reconciliation, complete trust account reconciliation, review property-level P&Ls, validate ownership allocations, and review exceptions with finance lead. ‍ Day 3–5 of New Month (Owner Statements Sent): Generate and review statements, send to owners via email or portal, and log and address owner questions. Mistake #8: No Visibility Into Property-Level Profitability Why is unit-level profitability the most important metric for scaling in 2026? Many property managers know their total revenue and total expenses, but not whether each individual property is actually profitable. This is one of the biggest blind spots in STR operations, and it quietly impacts owner retention, financial strategy, portfolio growth, and operational efficiency. Not all properties contribute equally. Some consume 2–3x more maintenance, guest services time, or housekeeping labor than others. A property can look fine in aggregate revenue but operate on razor-thin margins once true costs are allocated. The impacts are significant: high-maintenance homes erode overall margins, certain units act as loss-leaders, institutional owners expect property-level P&Ls, and renewal, pricing, and staffing decisions depend on accurate property-level data. Incorrect or unclear property-level expense allocation can result in inaccurate trust balances or owner liabilities—a subtle but critical compliance risk. Consider these real examples from actual portfolios: Property A generates $80K in annual revenue but has $75K in expenses, yielding only a 6% margin that barely covers operational overhead. Property B generates $40K in revenue with $25K in expenses, delivering a healthy 38% margin that subsidizes underperforming units. Aggregated reporting hides these realities completely and prevents you from making strategic decisions about pricing, renewals, or resource allocation. Commonly Missed Drivers of Profitability Several factors consistently slip through the cracks when managers try to assess true property-level performance: Labor Allocation: In-house maintenance, guest services, and on-call hours are rarely tracked by property, yet they materially impact margins. Owner Contract Structure: A 10% commission home with high maintenance may be unprofitable, while a 20% full-service home may outperform. Owner Behavior: Some owners require more requests, approvals, or custom work than others. Seasonality: Certain units consistently lose money in the off-season but carry the same fixed costs year-round. Without property-level visibility, PMs often keep or renew properties that quietly drag down financial performance. How to Fix It Build property-level visibility directly into your financial processes: Generate property-level P&Ls as part of your monthly close (or at minimum, quarterly) Track unit-level metrics: Cost per booking. Cost per clean. Maintenance % of revenue. Labor hours per property. Net Operating Income (NOI) after commissions. Conduct quarterly profitability reviews: Which units exceed your margin targets? Which require pricing or commission adjustments? Which should receive operational improvements? Which may need to be offboarded? Use this data to inform: Renewal and owner contract decisions. Pricing strategy. Staffing and resource allocation. Recommendations for CapEx improvements. Bottom line: If you don't know property-level profitability, you're not managing a portfolio—you're making decisions in the dark. The Financial Impact of Running Blind Without property-level visibility, operators unknowingly carry unprofitable units for years, sometimes decades. A typical scenario across the industry: 15-20% of properties in a portfolio operate at margins below 5%, consuming disproportionate operational resources, staff time, and management attention while appearing acceptable in aggregate reporting. For a 100-unit portfolio with $4M in annual revenue, those underperforming units can quietly drain $100,000-$200,000 in potential profit annually—money that should flow to your bottom line or be reinvested in growth. Operators who implement property-level P&Ls typically discover 3-5 units within their first quarter of analysis that should be repriced, renegotiated with owners on management fees, or offboarded entirely—decisions that improve overall portfolio margins by 3-8% within the first year. The time cost matters just as much: without clear profitability data, operator teams spend hours in circular debates about renewals, pricing adjustments, and resource allocation based on gut feel and anecdotes rather than data. Property-level reporting transforms these conversations from opinion-based arguments to data-driven strategy sessions where decisions are clear and defensible. Conclusion: Expense Discipline Is the New Superpower for STR Operators Every mistake on this list drains more than money—it drains trust, time, team morale, and your ability to scale confidently. As we head into 2026, the operators who thrive won't be the ones with the fanciest technology stack or the biggest portfolios. They'll be the ones who take control of their financial operations and make expense discipline a core competitive advantage. Because when your receipts are organized, your systems reconcile cleanly, your vendors stay in check, and your owner statements go out accurately and on time, everything in your business changes for the better. When you tighten your expense processes, everything upstream and downstream improves: Cleaner expense inputs. Faster, smoother closes. More accurate reporting. Clearer property-level profitability. More confident owners. Higher retention and more referrals. Healthier, more scalable margins. Financial clarity isn't just back-office hygiene anymore—it's a competitive advantage that separates growing, profitable operators from those stuck in survival mode. It's how operators protect margins, retain owners long-term, and scale with confidence instead of chaos. And here's the truth: you don't have to fix this alone. This is exactly why Topkey exists. We'll show you how Topkey gives operators the clarity and control they've been missing—without adding complexity to your day-to-day operations.

title: What to Share When Clients Ask for a Pentest Report?
summary: Even though clients intuitively ask for a pentest report, they are often not getting the right one. You are actually supposed to share the remediation report instead. This blog post explains why and what to share instead.
body_text: What to Share When Clients Ask for a Pentest Report? Written by Rene Brandel on Tue Jan 13 2026 When a security assessment concludes, the immediate instinct is to take the resulting document and pass it along to clients or partners as proof of due diligence. STOP . This is a common mistake in how these findings are communicated. Many organizations mistakenly share the "Deep-Dive Engineering Report" when they should be sharing the "Remediation Report" . This distinction is not just a matter of semantics. It fundamentally changes how your security posture is perceived by outside stakeholders. The internal engineering report is a technical manual designed for developers and systems administrators. It contains granular details about exploit strings, specific code vulnerabilities, and technical reproduction steps. While this is invaluable for your internal team, it is often too much information for a client. Sharing this level of detail can inadvertently expose the inner workings of your infrastructure. It creates more noise than clarity for someone who just needs to know if your platform is safe to use. The Power of the Remediation Report A remediation report serves a different purpose entirely. It communicates a narrative of responsibility and action. Instead of focusing on the "how" of a vulnerability, it focuses on the "what was done." This document shows that a weakness was identified and, more importantly, that it was successfully resolved. It demonstrates a mature security lifecycle where testing leads to concrete improvements rather than just a list of problems. Clients and auditors are looking for evidence of a functioning security program. When you provide a remediation report, you are showing them that your organization is proactive. It shifts the conversation from a snapshot of technical flaws to a long-term commitment to safety. This build-up of trust is essential in modern business where security is a primary concern for every procurement department. The Danger of the "Clean" Pentest Report There is a persistent myth that a "clean" pentest report with showing zero findings is the gold standard. In reality, a report with no findings often signals a lack of depth in the testing process rather than a perfect system. Modern software environments are far too complex for there to be zero vulnerabilities. A report showing no issues can actually raise red flags for sophisticated clients who understand the reality of cyber threats. A clean report suggests that the scope was too narrow or the methodology was not rigorous enough . It can look like a "check-the-box" exercise rather than a legitimate attempt to secure data. In contrast, a report that shows a dozen critical findings followed by proof of their remediation is far more impressive. It proves that you have the tools and the talent to find and fix the problems that actually exist. title: The Hard Truth About Expanding Your Cannabis Brand Into New States
summary: Scaling a cannabis brand isn’t like scaling traditional CPG. Every new state brings new rules, partners, and economics—making copy-and-paste expansion impossible. At Hall of Flowers, Nabis Co-CEO Jun Lee joined Embarc’s Dustin Moore and Equity Trade Network’s Ramon Garcia to break down what it really takes to grow into a multi-state cannabis brand. From choosing the right operational partners to navigating hidden market barriers, prioritizing specialization, and building for future interstate commerce, this conversation reveals the hard-earned strategies every cannabis operator needs before expanding into new markets.
body_text: Scaling a cannabis brand isn’t like scaling in traditional CPG. In this industry, crossing into every new state can be reset: new rules, new partners, new economics, and new customers. Copy-and-paste expansions don't work, and trying to brute-force your way into a market can burn cash and damage your brand.‍ At Hall of Flowers, a fireside chat featuring moderator Ramon Garcia of Equity Trade Network and speakers Dustin Moore, co-founder of Embarc, and Jun Lee, the Co-CEO and Co-Founder of Nabis, broke this challenge down with rare honesty. They revealed the same truth operators learn the hard way: You can win outside California, but only if you pick the right people, tackle the right barriers, and build on the proper foundation. Watch the full interview below and read the key takeaways for any brand looking to expand into new states. 1. Expansion Starts With People, Not Geography Before you pick a state, choose the partners who will help you operate there. As Jun put it, “We provide a railway for brands to access other markets with lower friction.” Relationships and the networks you build are infrastructure. 2. The Hardest Parts of Expansion Aren’t the Ones You Expect Some of the biggest challenges start after the licensing paperwork. Jun said, “If you’re going to New York, you have to find your suppliers, your manufacturers, then you have to build your retail relationships. It’s a very daunting task for an independent brand.” Most brands underestimate this. And it costs them. 3. Specialization Is the Most Underrated Advantage in Cannabis Expansion The strongest brands invest in: product story consumer experience …and outsource the rest. You can’t scale efficiently if you’re carrying unnecessary operational weight. 4. Expand Where You Have Pull — Not Where Everyone Else Is Pilgriming “Hot markets” are often hot because everyone rushes in, often without seeing the forest for the trees. A brand may succeed faster in a smaller, more aligned market than in a larger, more crowded one. The “obvious” next state isn’t always the right next state. 5. Advocacy Isn’t Optional — It’s Part of Your Expansion Strategy Regulation determines margins more than demand does. If you want to survive in a new market, you have to help shape it. Budget time for advocacy the same way you budget for inventory. Join coalitions, talk to regulators, support equity groups, and protect the markets you depend on. 6. Build With Today’s Borders, But Design for Interstate Commerce Build your systems now, assuming borders will fall when cannabis is federally legalized or descheduled. When they do, you want to be the brand already optimized for national flow. 7. Expansion Is a Team Sport — And the Best Teams Win Together Cannabis has always been a community-built industry. Before significant capital arrived, operators relied on collaborative shared survival. That hasn’t changed. Jun captured the ethos best: “It takes a village… and if there’s a shared vision, it’s much easier to build rapport and long-term value.”
